summary: Mobile Point's light at Fort Morgan, Alabama, lit in 1822 at the entrance to Mobile Bay: battle damage in 1864 and an iron tower now in storage.

access.note: Fort Morgan is open daily, with a small admission fee. Lighthouse Friends marks the tower as closed. The 1873 iron tower is in storage.

visit.note: Museum open 9 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. according to Lighthouse Friends; the site is closed on Thanksgiving, Christmas and New Year's Day.

events.note: Brick tower, forty feet per Lighthouse Friends (55 feet per the Encyclopedia of Alabama)
Lamps first lit 29 September 1822
Fixed light changed to a revolving light by a contractor (Winslow Lewis, per Lighthouse Friends) without instructions
Pair of range lights established near the main light
Fourth-order Fresnel lens installed (archive: original optic reflectors, later fourth-order Fresnel)
Downgraded to a harbor light after the Sand Island light took over as the landfall light (Encyclopedia of Alabama dates Sand Island to 1856)
After the war began, Confederate forces took the fort and the light was deactivated
Struck multiple times in the battle for the fort, 5 August 1864
Temporary wooden tower on the fort with a sixth-order lens, into service 2 September 1864 per Lighthouse Friends; the old brick tower demolished
Second iron tower, thirty feet, fixed red light first exhibited 15 February 1873 (the Encyclopedia of Alabama gives 1872)
Light changed from red to white
Brick oil house built, work begun 9 June and completed 12 June 1897
Light extinguished for a period during the Spanish-American War, when military rules barred ships from entering or leaving the bay at night
Storm report names a Mobile Point beacon, front range, as gone; this is a beacon, not the lighthouse
Hurricane of September 1926: Mobile Point Lighthouse, at Fort Morgan, slightly damaged
Modern steel skeletal tower erected at the point
Old iron tower taken down by a contractor and put in storage
Discontinued per the archive; the Encyclopedia of Alabama dates a federal replacement tower to 1966
Lighthouse put on the market by a Pensacola firm owned by the contractor; the contractor's son offered to donate the tower to the State of Alabama
Iron tower returned to Fort Morgan after federal funding for restoration was secured
Iron tower removed from the fort in September 2003 for restoration by Robinson Iron (the Encyclopedia of Alabama dates the dismantling to 2004)

corrections.why: The 1822 tower was brick (Lighthouse Friends calls it the old brick tower). The 9.1 m (30 ft) iron tower was built in 1873 (archive: Year Tower Established 1873; Lighthouse Friends: thirty-foot iron tower).

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Lighthouse Friends gives forty feet; the Encyclopedia of Alabama gives 55 feet. The story reports both.
The Encyclopedia of Alabama says a fourth-order lens from the start; Lighthouse Friends and the archive show reflectors, with the fourth-order Fresnel lens coming in 1858. The story reports both.
Lighthouse Friends gives 15 February 1873 and the archive gives 1873; the Encyclopedia of Alabama gives 1872.
Lighthouse Friends says thirty feet and the archive gives 30 ft from base to lantern; the Encyclopedia of Alabama says 50 feet. Story uses 30 ft.
Lighthouse Friends gives 2 September 1864 (during the war); the Encyclopedia of Alabama places it after the war.
Lighthouse Friends gives 1858; the Encyclopedia of Alabama gives 1856. The Sand Island light is a separate station and is mentioned only as the landfall replacement.

Lighthouse Friends says the steel tower was erected in 1963; the Encyclopedia of Alabama says the federal government replaced the 1872 structure in 1966. The archive gives 1966 as the discontinuance year.
Lighthouse Friends says September 2003; the Encyclopedia of Alabama says 2004.
The archive gives 1859 to 1861; Lighthouse Friends gives 1859 to 1862. The roster line follows the archive and the note gives the other date.
Lighthouse Friends gives both Alexander City and Alexandria City, Alabama. The story says only "in Alabama".

notes_for_editor: Naming and identity: the station record, the archive's MOBILE POINT (RANGE REAR) entry and the Wikipedia article for the range lights all describe this same site, and the sources here treat the 1822 Mobile Point light and the 1854 range pair as one station. The archive's Range Rear entry gives 1822 as established and 1873 as the tower date, so the light identified in the record as the 1822 iron tower is the 1873 tower (see corrections). The sources do not say which modern structure, if any, the Range A/Rear name refers to; the 1963 steel tower is the only later structure any source here ties to the point. Editor should confirm the naming before the page goes live. Keepers: the whole roster is the archive's compilation (NARA keeper registers via the archive), not checked against the registers. The only keeper confirmed in a second independent source here is Olsen (1909 newspaper letter). Annie F. Smith (1895-1896) appears only in the archive and in Lighthouse Friends, and I found no other record of her. Keepers and Coast Guard crew who served after about 1960 are in the roster only; the prose does not name them. Gaps: the Lighthouse Board annual reports in the corpus start in 1891 and the 1898 volume is missing, so the 1822 to 1889 history and the Spanish-American War darkening rest on Lighthouse Friends, the Encyclopedia of Alabama, Putnam and Weiss. Putnam's scan page 68 and the 1897 Board report page (scan page 383) were read from the OCR index and their printed page numbers were not checked against the images. The Montgomery Advertiser 1906 item names a beacon, not the light; it is kept as a storm entry with that caveat. The 1909 Olsen letter's subject is only partly reported. Lighthouse Friends is a copyrighted site: the story paraphrases it, and evidence quotes are internal. Wikipedia was read for leads only. The record's characteristic (Fl W 10s), focal height (38.1 m) and range (14 nm) are not supported by the history sources here and were not carried into facts. Fact-check 2026-10-28: the story now says 'miles' where Lighthouse Friends and the Encyclopedia of Alabama say miles (not nautical miles): the ten-mile visibility, the forty-five-mile Pensacola distance and the three-mile Sand Island distance. The iron tower's first light is given as 1873 (Lighthouse Friends and the archive) with the Encyclopedia's 1872 stated in the text. The archive's keeper years are copied as printed, including 'at least' (Thomas Harris 1831-1834; the list runs to at least 1970; James Chester Williams from at least 1924). The 1909 letter's subject is a worker who had left the construction force; the story does not name him. The links are hedged: the 1909 'Lighthouse Keeper Olsen of Mobile Point light' is tied to Hans J.G. Olsen only by station, surname and period; the Bulletin's 'Williams, J.C.' is tied to James C. Williams (archive and Lighthouse Friends) only as 'may be the same man'. Scan pages for the 1897 report (item 887, scan 383), Putnam (scan 68) and Weiss (scan 22) were confirmed against the corpus page index; the Bulletin pages (PDF 39 for the 1926 hurricane, PDF 36 for the index entry) were confirmed too.
